1 big thing: Lakers flip
By Dan Primack
 

Illustration: Lindsey Bailey/Axios

 

Across the NBA today, owners are smiling.

  • Venture capitalist Josh Kushner and former Disney CEO Bob Iger announced they've agreed to buy the Los Angeles Lakers at a $12.5 billion valuation.

🤑 Stunning stat: That's a 25% jump from where the team was valued just 10 months ago in Mark Walter's deal to buy it — still the most ever paid for a pro sports club.

The big picture: It's a dizzying ownership turnaround for the Lakers, one of pro sports' most iconic franchises.

  • Walter — who purchased a controlling stake from Jeanie Buss last October — today called owning the Lakers "one of the great honors of my life" and, in a massive understatement, "an extraordinary investment."

💵 Follow the money: Kushner and Iger would invest individually, with Kushner serving as the controlling owner, per a source.

  • The pair's sports-focused investment platform, Thrive Eternal, is expected to invest, but is limited by NBA rules to holding no more than a 20% stake.
  • Expect other investors to join the group.

What's next: This is only an agreement, not a finalized deal. It still needs league approval.

2. What's going on with CoreWeave
 
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

CoreWeave shares surged today after a second-quarter earnings report that seemed to tickle the market's fancy, Axios' Matt Phillips writes.

Why it matters: As a neocloud — a company that builds data centers and sells AI compute — CoreWeave can say a lot about both the unit economics of AI and the market vibe on the technology.

📊 The latest: Demand seemed strong.

  • Sales more than doubled, to $2.58 billion.
  • Remaining performance obligations — a measure of sales backlog — jumped 245%, to $103.7 billion.

📉 Yes, but: The company's expenses are growing too — along with its losses.

  • Its adjusted net loss worsened to $567 million from $130 million during the same quarter last year.

👋 The intrigue: It's likely the gangbusters stock move after the earnings report — it jumped 19% — had something to do with the large short position embedded in CoreWeave.

  • Recent data showed more than 20% of its float was in the hands of shorts, who must repurchase shares to exit their trades, a technical feature that can cause a sudden run-up in share prices, known as a short squeeze, when shorts exit a trade en masse.

3. 🥬 Lettuce prices wilt
 
Data: BLS series CUSR0000SEFL02; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals

Lettuce is experiencing an explosive decline in stores.

  • The cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce has sparked a massive drop in prices, as consumers steered clear of supermarket lettuce bins.

📉 By the numbers: CPI numbers released today by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that lettuce prices plunged 16.4% from June to July.

  • That was the largest decline ever, by a long shot.
 
 
4. Other happenings
 

A Wendy's restaurant in New York. Photo: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto via Getty Images

 

🍔 Activist investor Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management is considering an offer to acquire Wendy's. The fast-food chain has been struggling to keep up with its rivals. (FT)

💉Eli Lilly filed six lawsuits accusing companies of selling illegal versions of its promising obesity drug retatrutide, which is still in clinical trials. (CNBC)

🛠️ Home Depot CEO Ted Decker is taking a temporary leave of absence for medical reasons for "the next few months." CFO Richard McPhail and Ann-Marie Campbell, senior VP of U.S. stores and operations, will oversee the company while he's gone. (WSJ)

 
 
5. 🎙️ Alex Cooper's Unwell lands investment
 

Unwell co-CEO and co-founder Alex Cooper and WTSL CEO Patrick Whitesell. Photo: Courtesy of Michela Pini, Unwell

 

Unwell, the media company co-founded by "Call Her Daddy" host Alex Cooper and Matt Kaplan, has secured its first investment at a $500 million pre-money valuation, Axios Pro's Kerry Flynn writes.

  • WTSL, the investment firm led by former Endeavor executive Patrick Whitesell and Jason Lublin, is making the strategic investment. The amount of capital being invested was not disclosed.

Zoom out: Unwell's podcast network now hosts more than a dozen shows and partners with SiriusXM. The company produces film and TV shows, hosts live events and runs a creative agency.

  • Unwell also sells consumer products, including hydration and energy drinks.

The investment comes after a June Vanity Fair investigation reported allegations of a toxic workplace and volatile behavior by Kaplan.

  • They've denied the allegations.
